chunks.section: CAST: History-Adaptive Spectral Clipping for LLM Pretraining
chunks.text: Jiacheng Li Jianchao Tan † † thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Kefeng Zhang, Yuchen Xie, Xunliang Cai Affiliation: Meituan, Beijing, China Affiliation: {lijiacheng14, tanjianchao02}@meituan.com

Soft spectral clipping (SSC) reduces gradient singular values, but its effect depends on the gradient scale and clipping threshold. We introduce CAST (Clipping with Adaptive Scales and Thresholds), a history-adaptive extension of SSC. AdamW’s previous second moment sets row and column scales. An exponential moving average of the clipped output’s estimated spectral norm sets each matrix’s threshold. CAST restores the original coordinates before the AdamW update. We train a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 19.08B total parameters for 83.89B tokens. CAST achieves lower training and mean validation losses than nine gradient-processing baselines, with the fewest relative gradient spikes. It reaches the best baseline’s final smoothed training loss in 7.2% fewer steps.

Gradient clipping ( Zhang et al., 2020 ) controls large gradients during language model ( Team et al., 2025b ; Brown et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026 ; Team et al., 2025a ; Team et al., 2026 ) pretraining ( Pascanu et al., 2013 ) . When applied before AdamW, it also changes the moment estimates used by later updates ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) . The clipping rule therefore affects both the current update and the optimizer’s state over time. Global norm clipping rescales the whole gradient by a single factor. This limits the influence of an unusually large gradient while preserving its direction. A matrix gradient can be large mainly along a few directions. Rescaling the entire matrix then also weakens other directions, even when their magnitudes are already moderate. Spectral clipping controls the gradient magnitude in each singular direction. SPECTRA ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) develops a smooth spectral transformation for application before or after a base optimizer ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ; Kingma and Ba, 2017 ; Jordan et al., 2024 ) . We use pre-optimizer SSC (SSC-Pre) because CAST also acts on gradients before AdamW. We label its constant and cosine threshold schedules SSC-constant and SSC-cosine.

A clipping threshold is meaningful only relative to the gradient scale. Persistent differences in row and column magnitudes affect the spectrum on which clipping acts. An unusually large value in one part of a matrix may be routine in another, and the overall scale can change over training. A fixed threshold may therefore apply different clipping strengths as the gradient scale changes. SPECTRA’s decaying pre-clipping threshold shows the value of adjusting this threshold during training. Such a schedule depends on the training step. A history-based rule can instead respond to changes in each matrix. We therefore use each matrix’s history to set its gradient scale and clipping threshold. 1. Dashed histories advance only after a successful update. We introduce CAST (Clipping with Adaptive Scales and Thresholds), which uses two complementary histories (Figure 2 ). Historical scaling (HS) uses row and column summaries of AdamW’s previous second moment to set the scale for each gradient matrix. SSC acts in these standardized coordinates, and the output returns to its original scale before updating AdamW. AdamW updates both moments from this restored gradient. The updated second moment supplies the scale used at the next step.

We also maintain an exponential moving average (EMA) of the clipped output’s estimated spectral norm, computed in the same standardized coordinates. This estimate measures the largest singular value after clipping. The previous EMA sets the current threshold before clipping begins. CAST retains SSC’s soft map and Newton–Schulz routine. The two histories control the input coordinates and clipping threshold. Our contributions are threefold: • Historical scaling. We use row and column summaries of the previous second moment to define the coordinates of spectral clipping. We then restore the gradient’s original scale. • Output feedback. We adapt each matrix’s threshold to its clipped output history, so the threshold follows changes in the clipped spectrum. • Pretraining results. CAST achieves the lowest training and mean validation losses among nine baselines in our MoE study (Figure 1 ). We examine its component effects, gradient dynamics, and training cost.

SPECTRA is the direct starting point for this work ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) . It smoothly reduces singular values through a matrix inverse square root, computed with Newton–Schulz iterations ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . Its framework combines spectral clipping of optimizer updates with optional gradient preprocessing. This gradient preprocessing forms the SSC baselines in our study. SPECTRA also studies how the clipping threshold changes during training. Its pre-clipping study compares a fixed threshold of 0.1 with cosine decay from 10 to 0.01. The decaying schedule gives better results. We use the previous second moment to set the clipping scale and the complete clipped output to update the threshold. We retain full-matrix soft clipping throughout. Section 5.1 describes our SSC baselines.

Adafactor represents second moments through row and column statistics ( Shazeer and Stern, 2018 ) . Our scale uses the same factored structure, with positive floors, to define the coordinates of spectral clipping. AdamW keeps its full moment states and uses the gradient after we restore its original scale. AdaGC adapts per-tensor thresholds from previous clipped norms ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . Our spectral history follows this output-based principle for each matrix. It uses an estimated spectral norm in standardized coordinates. Parameters outside the spectral branch use an output-norm controller. ZClip uses running global norm statistics to detect spikes ( Kumar et al., 2025 ) . GradientStabilizer transforms global magnitude using two scalar moving averages ( Huang et al., 2026 ) . These histories track different quantities from AdamW’s coordinatewise second moment. Other transformations use current parameter or gradient magnitudes. AGC bounds unitwise gradient norms relative to parameter norms ( Brock et al., 2021 ) ; coordinate clipping bounds individual entries. GradPower applies a signed elementwise power before the optimizer ( Wang et al., 2026b ) . These methods cover global, tensor, coordinate, and spectral gradient processing.

We evaluate pretraining quality, component effects, and training cost over 5,000 steps (83.89B nominal tokens).

We train a shortcut MoE model ( Cai et al., 2025 ) with 10 blocks, hidden size 1536, and 16 attention heads ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) . Each block contains two multi-head latent attention modules ( DeepSeek-AI et al., 2024 ) , two dense SwiGLU modules, and one MoE module ( Shazeer et al., 2017 ; Fedus et al., 2022 ; Jiang et al., 2024 ) . The model structure gives approximately 19.08B total parameters. Its target activated backbone has 647.6M parameters, excluding input and output embeddings. Actual expert activation depends on routing. The full calculation appears in Appendix C . The runs share the recorded data and tokenizer configurations. We use sequence length 8192, global batch size 2048, microbatch size 1, and training seed 48. AdamW uses ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0.9 , 0.95 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.95) , ϵ = 10 − 16 \epsilon=10^{-16} , and weight decay 0.1. The learning rate reaches 8 × 10 − 4 8\times 10^{-4} after 500 warmup iterations and remains constant through the comparison window. Training uses BF16 and expert parallelism of eight. The model, optimizer fields, and recorded learning-rate trajectory agree across the conditions.

We compare with GlobalGC, AdaGC, SSC-constant, SSC-cosine, GradientStabilizer, GradPower, ClipByValue, AGC, and ZClip. Appendix C.2 gives each baseline’s processing order and hyperparameters. Both SSC baselines use five Newton–Schulz iterations on the same selected matrices in raw coordinates. SSC-constant uses τ = 0.1 \tau=0.1 . SSC-cosine decays τ \tau from 10 to 0.1 over 5,000 steps. Input-gradient spikes mark abrupt increases before clipping. Figure 6 shows these norms after learning-rate warmup. We count norms above 1 and relative spikes. A relative spike exceeds twice the preceding 100-step median, including pre-window points when needed. Both counts include consecutive exceedances. Relative spikes track sudden increases against each run’s recent gradient scale. The absolute count applies the same norm threshold across runs. CAST recorded one relative spike and no input norm above 1 during iterations 501–5000. SSC-constant and SSC-cosine recorded 22 and 21 relative spikes, respectively (Table 3 ). CAST and SSC-constant had similar median norms, while CAST had a smaller upper tail. Among the baselines, GradPower had the lowest median norm but 422 relative spikes. ZClip had the largest isolated norm, at 918.79, and 75 relative spikes. AdaGC had six relative spikes and a lower 99th-percentile norm than CAST. CAST combines the fewest relative spikes with the lowest mean validation loss. Cosine decay reduced the fixed-threshold variant’s relative spikes from six to two and norms above 1 from 194 to 21.

Table 4 compares 64-device runs on the same hardware type. Each device has about 60% of an NVIDIA H100’s compute capacity. CAST takes 2.0% longer per step than SSC-constant and 1.9% longer than ClipByValue. Timings include execution and logging and vary with cluster load. AdaGC has the lowest final smoothed loss among the baselines. CAST first reaches this loss at step 4,639, using 7.2% fewer steps (Figure 7 ). At the mean step times in Table 4 , reaching AdaGC’s loss target takes an estimated 5.5% less time than 5,000 ClipByValue steps. CAST uses two histories to guide spectral clipping in pretraining. AdamW’s previous second moment sets the gradient scale. An EMA of the clipped output’s estimated spectral norm sets each matrix’s threshold. In 5,000-step MoE pretraining, CAST achieved lower training and mean validation losses than nine baselines and three component variants. It also had the fewest relative gradient spikes. CAST reached AdaGC’s final smoothed loss in 7.2% fewer steps. Including per-step overhead, the estimated time saving is 5.5% relative to 5,000 ClipByValue steps. These results support using both histories to improve pretraining quality and efficiency.

Full-matrix computation and communication times depend on tensor shape. The reported timings also reflect the cluster environment. Changes in hardware or training settings can also change the exact speedup. The timing comparison uses the same model, training settings, hardware type, and device count. This shared setup supports a fair comparison, so the estimated relative speedup remains a useful reference.
